title: When should you repartition after a highly-filtered DataFrame (many empty/tiny partitions → repartition to rebalance), and when should you coalesce before writing output (reduce small files)?
shortTitle: When to repartition after a heavy filter vs coalesce before writing output

s1_definition.profdef: After a highly selective filter, a DataFrame keeps the same number of partitions it started with, but most of them become nearly empty while a few hold the surviving rows, so repartition is used to rebalance into fewer, evenly sized partitions and restore efficient parallelism. Before writing output, coalesce is used to reduce the number of partitions so the job does not emit hundreds of tiny files, which hurt downstream read performance and overload the file system with metadata. The first is a rebalancing problem solved by a shuffle; the second is a file-count problem solved by a cheap narrow merge.
s1_definition.analogy: Suppose the National Bank of India starts with two hundred clerks each holding a stack of transaction slips. A filter keeping only fraud alerts leaves ninety-nine percent of clerks with empty hands and one clerk buried under slips. Repartition re-deals so every clerk has a fair share again. Later, when filing the final report, writing one tiny file per clerk floods the records room with two hundred almost-empty folders, so you coalesce the stacks into ten tidy folders before filing.
s1_definition.oneliner: Repartition after a heavy filter to rebalance skewed partitions; coalesce before writing to avoid a flood of tiny files.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** After a highly selective filter, a DataFrame keeps the same number of partitions it started with, but most of them become nearly empty while a few hold the surviving rows, so repartition is used to rebalance into fewer, evenly sized partitions and restore efficient parallelism. Before writing output, coalesce is used to reduce the number of partitions so the job does not emit hundreds of tiny files, which hurt downstream read performance and overload the file system with metadata. The first is a rebalancing problem solved by a shuffle; the second is a file-count problem solved by a cheap narrow merge.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Suppose the National Bank of India starts with two hundred clerks each holding a stack of transaction slips. A filter keeping only fraud alerts leaves ninety-nine percent of clerks with empty hands and one clerk buried under slips. Repartition re-deals so every clerk has a fair share again. Later, when filing the final report, writing one tiny file per clerk floods the records room with two hundred almost-empty folders, so you coalesce the stacks into ten tidy folders before filing.

**One line to remember:** Repartition after a heavy filter to rebalance skewed partitions; coalesce before writing to avoid a flood of tiny files.

sections.s2_technical:
A filter in Spark is a narrow transformation. It does not change the partition count; it simply drops rows inside each existing partition. So if you start with two hundred partitions and keep only one percent of rows, you still have two hundred partitions, but most are nearly empty and a couple may be large. This is bad for the next stage because Spark still schedules two hundred tasks, most doing almost nothing, which wastes scheduling overhead, and any downstream wide operation shuffles two hundred partitions needlessly. Calling `repartition(n)` with a smaller, sensible `n` performs a shuffle that evens the survivors into balanced partitions, so the next stage runs efficiently. You accept the shuffle cost because the alternative — hundreds of lopsided tasks — is worse.

Before writing, the concern is different. Each partition becomes one output file. If you have two hundred partitions but only a little data, you write two hundred tiny files. Tiny files are a well-known problem: object stores and HDFS pay a fixed cost per file, listing and opening many files is slow, and downstream readers lose efficiency because small files defeat columnar read optimizations. Here you call `coalesce(n)` to merge down to a reasonable file count. Coalesce is correct because it is cheap and there is usually no heavy work between the merge and the write, so the narrow merge does not collapse any important parallelism.

The distinction is which problem you are solving. Repartition after a filter fixes skewed, wasteful parallelism and is worth a shuffle. Coalesce before write fixes the small-file problem and avoids paying for a shuffle you do not need. A senior-level nuance is that if you also need the output sorted or evenly sized files, you repartition before writing instead of coalescing; and if there is heavy computation right before the write, coalescing to a tiny number can serialize that work, in which case repartition is safer.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India scans two hundred partitions of the day's transactions to find suspected fraud. The fraud filter keeps only a tiny fraction, leaving two hundred partitions that are almost all empty. The next step enriches each surviving alert with customer data — a shuffle-join. Running it over two hundred mostly-empty partitions means two hundred tasks for a handful of rows. This is exactly where `repartition(4)` helps — rebalance the survivors into four even partitions so the join runs with four efficient tasks.

Problem 2 — After enrichment, the alerts must be written to the data lake. If written as-is, the job emits many tiny files. This is exactly where `coalesce(1)` or `coalesce(2)` before write helps — merge the small result into one or two files so the lake is not polluted with tiny files, and because there is no heavy work between the merge and the write, the cheap narrow coalesce is safe.

The demo models partition occupancy before and after a selective filter, recommends repartition to rebalance, then recommends coalesce before the write, logging partition counts and file counts at each step.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the demo
java -cp target/spark-fraud-partition-service-1.0.0.jar com.bank.spark.FraudPartitionDemo

# In a real Spark job:
#   alerts = txns.filter(col("fraudScore") > 0.9)   # 200 partitions, mostly empty
#   balanced = alerts.repartition(4)                 # rebalance survivors (shuffle)
#   enriched = balanced.join(customers, "accountId") # efficient 4-task join
#   enriched.coalesce(2).write.parquet("s3://.../fraud-alerts")  # avoid tiny files
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: 200 partitions of transactions; a fraud filter keeps 300 rows spread unevenly across just three partitions.

Step 1: The filter runs as a narrow transformation. The partition count stays at 200, but 197 partitions are now empty and three hold the 300 survivors — a badly skewed, wasteful layout.

Step 2: The advisor inspects occupancy, sees 197 empty partitions and 300 surviving rows, and recommends `repartition(4)`. A shuffle redistributes the 300 rows into four balanced partitions, so the next enrichment join runs with four efficient tasks instead of 200 mostly-idle ones.

Step 3: The enrichment join runs on the four balanced partitions, producing the enriched alerts.

Step 4: Before writing, the advisor computes a file count targeting about 1000 rows per file. With 300 alerts that is one file, so it recommends `coalesce(1)` (or `coalesce(2)` for safety), a cheap narrow merge that avoids emitting many tiny files.

Step 5: The job writes the coalesced output to the data lake.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 04:23:50 [WARNING] After fraud filter: 200 partitions, 197 empty, 300 surviving rows
2026-10-30 04:23:50 [INFO] Recommend repartition(3) to rebalance survivors for the enrichment join
2026-10-30 04:23:50 [INFO] Recommend coalesce(1) before write to avoid tiny files (300 alerts, ~1000 rows/file)
2026-10-30 04:23:50 [INFO] Flow: filter -> repartition(rebalance) -> enrich join -> coalesce -> write
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
These are two different problems that happen to both involve partition counts. A filter in Spark is a narrow transformation, so it never changes the number of partitions — it only drops rows inside each one. That means a highly selective filter leaves you with the same large number of partitions, but most are nearly empty while a few hold the survivors. That layout is wasteful because Spark still schedules a task per partition and any downstream wide operation shuffles all of them. So after a heavy filter I repartition to a small, sensible number, accepting the shuffle cost because it rebalances the survivors into evenly sized partitions and restores efficient parallelism.

The second problem is at write time. Each partition becomes one output file, so if I write without reducing the count I emit a flood of tiny files, which object stores and HDFS handle poorly — fixed cost per file, slow listings, and defeated columnar read optimizations downstream. So before writing I coalesce to a reasonable file count. Coalesce is the right tool here because it is a cheap narrow merge and there is usually no heavy computation between the merge and the write, so it does not collapse any important parallelism.

In my fraud pipeline at the National Bank of India this was the exact flow. The fraud filter left two hundred partitions almost all empty with the few survivors clustered in two or three partitions, so I repartitioned to four to rebalance before the enrichment join, which turned two hundred mostly-idle tasks into four efficient ones. Then, because the alert volume was small, I coalesced to one or two partitions before writing so the data lake received a couple of tidy files instead of two hundred tiny ones. The way I summarize it in interviews is: repartition after a selective filter to fix skewed parallelism, and coalesce before writing to fix the small-file problem — and if there is heavy work right before the write, repartition instead so coalesce does not serialize it.
